how.intro: QuietLink encrypts your text in your browser before it leaves your device. This page explains what happens and what the server can—and cannot—do.
how.flow.title: From your device to the recipient
how.flow.step1.title: Your browser encrypts the text
how.flow.step1.body: A random key is created locally. The text is encrypted before the application sends anything to the server.
how.flow.step2.title: The server stores unreadable data
how.flow.step2.body: The server stores the ciphertext and the minimum metadata needed for expiration, access proofs and deletion.
how.flow.step3.title: The recipient decrypts locally
how.flow.step3.body: The recipient's browser uses the key from the link to decrypt and display the text. The plaintext stays in the browser.
how.server.title: What stays private
how.server.sees.title: The server can receive
how.server.sees.item2: Public settings: expiry, read-once mode, whether a passphrase is used (with its salt and Argon2id parameters) and the encrypted size, which reveals the approximate text length.
how.server.sees.item3: Public cryptographic proofs needed to serve the content.
how.server.sees.item4: A hash of the deletion token, never the token itself.
how.server.sees.item5: Your IP address, for rate limiting; only a keyed hash renewed daily is kept.
how.server.never.title: The server never receives
how.server.never.item2: The key after the # in the share URL.
how.server.never.item3: Your passphrase or any secret key derived from it.
how.link.title: Understand the share link
how.link.exampleExplanation: Everything before # may be sent to the server. The fragment after # stays in the browser and is used locally for decryption.
how.options.title: Security options
how.options.item1: Expiration removes the content after a chosen duration.
how.options.item2: Read once reserves the content and destroys its payload after confirmation.
how.options.item3: An optional passphrase adds a local Argon2id-derived key.
how.options.item4: The deletion link lets its holder request permanent deletion.
how.options.item5: Markdown and code are rendered locally; no external preview service is contacted.
how.options.item6: No account or file upload is needed.
how.readOnce.title: How read-once works
how.readOnce.step1: Someone opens the link and chooses “{action}”.
how.readOnce.step2: The browser checks the passphrase locally, when one is configured.
how.readOnce.step3: QuietLink reserves the content so another reader cannot open it at the same time.
how.readOnce.step4: After successful confirmation, the encrypted payload is removed from the server.
how.readOnce.limit: Limit: someone who has the link but not the passphrase cannot read the text, but by failing the confirmation several times they can cause it to be destroyed.
how.trust.title: Important trust limit
how.faq.title: Frequently asked questions
how.faq.q1: Can the server read my text?
how.faq.a1: No. The text is encrypted in your browser before it is sent. However, an operator who can replace the application's JavaScript could attempt to capture a key when a user creates or reads content. Use an instance you trust.
how.faq.q2: What happens if I share the link?
how.faq.a2: Anyone who has the share link can try to read the content. Send the link only to the intended recipient and send any passphrase through a different channel.
how.faq.q3: Why should I not test a read-once link myself?
how.faq.a3: Opening the link starts the read-once flow. If you are the creator, use the warning on the result screen and send the link without opening it first.
how.faq.q4: What if I lose the deletion link?
how.faq.a4: The content can still expire or be consumed normally, but you may no longer be able to request manual deletion. Keep the deletion link private and separate from the share link.
how.faq.a5: No. Unpublished text is not saved automatically in browser storage, cookies, the URL or a third-party service.
how.faq.q6: What if the server is compromised?
how.faq.a6: A storage leak should expose ciphertext rather than plaintext. A server that can alter the JavaScript served to browsers is a different threat and can try to capture keys at runtime.
